mainTopic: Cutting trees and the deadlines for eating שביעית produce, signs of land types, and local customs about selling animals and roasted meat on פסח night
overview: This amud opens at the end of a ברייתא about when it becomes forbidden to cut down fruit trees during שביעית. רב אסי says that בוסר and גירוע are the same stage, reached when the grape is the size of a white bean. The גמרא then rejects its earlier explanation of how רבי אילעאי could cut down a palm tree, and concludes that the tree's dates never ripen on the tree. Next, a ברייתא lists how long one may keep eating each kind of שביעית fruit: until that fruit is gone from late-ripening places like אוכל, תקוע, בית הִינֵי and צוער. Another source gives holiday deadlines instead. The גמרא answers that both describe the same time, and that the real test is whether the fruit is still found in the field. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל then lists plants that mark each kind of land, and the גמרא explains their uses for בכורים, עגלה ערופה, and buying and selling. A new משנה follows about local customs: selling animals to non-Jews and eating roasted meat on פסח night. The גמרא brings רב's rule against saying 'this meat is for פסח,' and challenges it from the story of תודוס of Rome. The discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the list: when vines, olives and other trees become forbidden to cut
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא (which began on the previous amud) finishes its list of when it becomes forbidden to cut down trees in שביעית. Vines are forbidden once their grapes form kernels, olive trees once they blossom, and all other trees once they produce fruit.
steps.simpleTranslation: [Vines may not be cut down] from when the grapes form kernels; olive trees, from when they blossom; and all other trees, from when they produce fruit.
steps.whatsHappening: We are in the middle of a ברייתא that lists, tree by tree, the point from which you may not cut down a fruit tree during שביעית. This amud picks up with its last three items.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each tree gets its own stage of growth that counts as 'having fruit.' Once a tree reaches that stage, cutting it down would destroy שביעית fruit, so it is forbidden. The general rule for all other trees is simply 'once they produce fruit.'

keyTerms.meaning: From when (the grapes) form kernels and swell a little

steps.confusionAlert: This amud starts mid-sentence. The subject of 'משיגריעו' is the grapevine, which was named in the part of the ברייתא that came on the previous amud.

phrases.english: from when [the grapes] form kernels;
phrases.notes: The ברייתא is still going here; this line is talking about grapevines.

phrases.english: and olive trees, from when they blossom;
and all other trees, from when they produce fruit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a ברייתא begun on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In שביעית, vines may not be cut once grapes form kernels, olive trees once they blossom, and other trees once they produce fruit.

steps.title: רב אסי: unripe grape, grape kernel and white bean are one stage
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי teaches that בוסר and גירוע are the same stage, and links that stage to פול הלבן.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב אסי said: It is בוסר, it is גירוע, it is a white bean.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אסי explains the word 'גירוע' from the ברייתא. He says it is the same stage as בוסר, and he connects it to a white bean.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This tells us that the ברייתא's 'משיגריעו' is the very stage that other sources call בוסר. As the next step shows, the mention of a white bean is confusing as worded.

keyTerms.meaning: An unripe grape, at the early stage of grape growth
A grape that has formed a kernel and begun to swell

phrases.english: And Rav Asi said:
It is an unripe grape, it is a grape kernel,
it is a white bean.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the term גירוע from the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בוסר and גירוע are one and the same stage of grape growth.

steps.title: Can a grape really be called a white bean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is puzzled: a grape is never a white bean, so how can רב אסי say 'it is a white bean'?
steps.simpleTranslation: A white bean — could that enter your mind?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the wording of רב אסי's statement. A grape at any stage is obviously not a bean.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taken literally, the third clause makes no sense. The challenge is aimed only at the wording, not at the ruling that בוסר and גירוע are the same, and it sets up a corrected reading.

keyTerms.meaning: Could it enter your mind? (an expression of disbelief)

phrases.english: A white bean — does that enter your mind?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the literal wording of רב אסי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'הוא פול הלבן' in רב אסי's statement.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A grape cannot literally be a bean, so the statement cannot mean what it says.

steps.title: Correction: the grape is the size of a white bean
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads רב אסי: he meant that בוסר is about as big as a white bean.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: its size is like a white bean.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the wording. The bean is a measure of size, not an identity.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now רב אסי gives a practical measure. Once the grapes reach the size of a white bean, they count as בוסר / גירוע, and from then on the vine may not be cut in שביעית.
steps.whatToRemember: בוסר = גירוע = a grape about the size of a white bean.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
its size is like a white bean.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב אסי seemed to say the grape is a bean.
steps.terutzMaskana: He meant the בוסר stage is reached when the grape is the size of a white bean.

steps.title: The Rabbis themselves forbid cutting once any fruit appears
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges its earlier answer about רבי אילעאי. That answer said he followed רבנן, who hold that סמדר is not yet fruit. But this same ברייתא of רבנן forbids cutting all other trees once they produce anything.
steps.simpleTranslation: And whom did you hear say 'בוסר yes, סמדר no'? The Rabbis. Yet they teach: all other trees, from when they produce fruit!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to an earlier explanation of how רבי אילעאי could cut down a palm tree. It shows that the ברייתא we just read contradicts that explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא said רבי אילעאי cut a tree at the סמדר stage, following רבנן who say סמדר is not real fruit. But in our ברייתא, רבנן (the opinion of בית הלל) forbid cutting other trees as soon as they produce fruit at all. So even early fruit like dates at the bud stage would forbid cutting, and the old answer collapses.

keyTerms.meaning: The bud or blossom stage of fruit, before בוסר
And yet it teaches (introduces a contradicting source)
The Sages (here: those who argue with רבי יוסי)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a challenge to רב אסי. It attacks the earlier explanation of רבי אילעאי's action, which came earlier.

phrases.english: And whom did you hear who said:
an unripe grape, yes [it is fruit]; a bud, no?
The Rabbis.
And it teaches [in their name]:
all other trees, from when they produce fruit!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the ברייתא of step 1 to undo an earlier explanation of רבי אילעאי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier answer that רבי אילעאי cut a tree at the סמדר stage, following רבנן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבנן forbid cutting other trees from the moment they produce anything, so even סמדר-stage dates would forbid cutting.

steps.title: רבי אילעאי cut a tree with dates that never ripen on it
steps.stepSummary: New answer: רבי אילעאי cut a palm whose dates were דניסחני, a stunted kind that never ripens on the tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי אילעאי cut [a palm] with stunted dates.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops its earlier answer and gives a new one. The tree רבי אילעאי cut had dates that never ripen while still on the tree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since these dates only ripen after being picked, the tree is not considered to be producing fruit in the normal sense. Cutting it down does not destroy fruit growing on the tree, so it is permitted even according to רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: Stunted dates that never ripen on the tree
An early אמורא whose action is being explained

steps.whatToRemember: רבי אילעאי's cutting was allowed only because the dates were a stunted kind that never ripens on the tree, not because buds don't count.

phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi Elai
cut [a tree] with stunted dates.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by redefining the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי אילעאי cut a tree at the סמדר stage because buds are not fruit.
steps.terutzMaskana: He cut a tree whose dates never ripen on the tree, so it was not a fruit-producing tree in the forbidden sense.

steps.title: Grapes may be eaten until the vines of אוכל are empty
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא about how long one may eat שביעית fruit before ביעור. Grapes may be eaten until the vines in אוכל have none left, or later if some place still has grapes after אוכל.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: One may eat grapes until the vine branches of אוכל are finished. If there are later ones than those, one may eat on their account.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא listing deadlines for eating שביעית produce. It begins with grapes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is tied to when that fruit is gone from the field everywhere. אוכל is named only because its grapes are usually the last. If later grapes exist elsewhere, the eating time is extended.

keyTerms.meaning: Vine branches trained on a trellis
Until they are finished or gone

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the principle behind ביעור: you may eat a fruit as long as that fruit is still available in the field. The places named are examples, not fixed limits.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
One may eat grapes
until the vine branches of Okhel are finished.
If there are later ones than those,
one may eat on their account.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic: deadlines for eating שביעית produce (ביעור).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Grapes may be eaten until they are gone from the latest place, normally Okhel.

steps.title: Olives: until the last in תקוע, or in גוש חלב per רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: Olives may be eaten until the last olives in תקוע are gone. רבי אליעזר says until the last olives in גוש חלב are gone.
steps.simpleTranslation: One may eat olives until the last in תקוע is finished. רבי אליעזר says: until the last of גוש חלב is finished.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with olives and records a disagreement about which town's olives set the deadline.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree on the principle that the last place to have olives sets the limit. They disagree about which place is truly last: the תנא קמא says תקוע, and רבי אליעזר says גוש חלב.

keyTerms.meaning: Tekoa, a town known for olives
Gush Chalav, a town in the Galil

phrases.english: One may eat olives
until the last [olive] in Tekoa is finished.
Rabbi Eliezer says:

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁיִּכְלֶה אַחֲרוֹן שֶׁל גּוּשׁ חָלָב,
phrases.english: until the last of Gush Chalav is finished,

steps.triggerLanguage: אוֹכְלִים בְּזֵיתִים עַד שֶׁיִּכְלֶה אַחֲרוֹן שֶׁבִּתְקוֹעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Olives may be eaten until they are gone from תקוע (תנא קמא) or from גוש חלב (רבי אליעזר).

steps.title: When fruit counts as 'finished': a poor person can't find a רובע
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא defines 'finished': a poor person searching would not find a רובע of olives, either on the branches or fallen near the trunk.
steps.simpleTranslation: So that a poor person goes out and does not find, neither on its branches nor at its base, a רובע.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a practical test for when the olives count as 'finished' in that town.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Finished' does not mean that not one olive remains. It means a poor person could not gather even a רובע, either from the treetop or from fallen fruit by the trunk. Below that amount, the fruit is considered gone.

keyTerms.meaning: A quarter-kav, a measure of volume

steps.whatToRemember: Fruit is 'finished' for ביעור when a poor person would not find a רובע on or under the trees.

phrases.english: [that is,] so that a poor person goes out
and does not find,
neither in its branches nor at its trunk,
a quarter-kav.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּדֵי שֶׁיְּהֵא עָנִי יוֹצֵא וְאֵינוֹ מוֹצֵא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines what 'finished' (שיכלה) means.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Fruit is finished when a poor person cannot find a רובע on the tree or beneath it.

steps.title: Dried figs: until the unripe figs of בית הִינֵי are gone
steps.stepSummary: Dried figs may be eaten until the unripe figs of בית הִינֵי are gone from the trees.
steps.simpleTranslation: One may eat dried figs until the unripe figs of בית הִינֵי are finished.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues its list with dried figs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The figs of בית הִינֵי ripen very late, so their disappearance marks the end of figs in the field. Once they are gone, the time to eat stored dried figs ends as well.

keyTerms.meaning: Beit Hini, a place with late-ripening figs

phrases.english: One may eat dried figs
until the unripe figs of Beit Hini are finished.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the ברייתא's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dried figs may be eaten until the late unripe figs of בית הִינֵי are gone.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: בית הִינֵי figs belong to the laws of מעשר
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says the unripe figs of בית הִינֵי were only ever mentioned for the laws of מעשר, not for שביעית.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה said: The unripe figs of בית הִינֵי were mentioned only regarding מעשר.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees with the line we just learned in Step 10, which used the unripe figs of בית הִינֵי as the time limit for dried figs. He says these figs were only discussed for the laws of מעשר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 used the figs of בית הִינֵי to set the deadline for eating dried figs in שביעית. רבי יהודה says they cannot serve as a sign for that deadline. As far as he knows, the only law said about them is about מעשר.

keyTerms.meaning: A place whose figs never fully ripen on the tree

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said:
The unripe figs of Beit Hini were not mentioned
except regarding tithes.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה: לֹא הוּזְכְּרוּ פַּגֵּי בֵּית הִינֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disputes the use of בית הִינֵי figs as the שביעית time marker from Step 10
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The figs of בית הִינֵי are a topic of מעשר, not a sign for the שביעית deadline

steps.title: The משנה about בית הִינֵי figs and טוֹבִינָא dates
steps.stepSummary: The source for רבי יהודה is a משנה that says the figs of בית הִינֵי and the dates of טוֹבִינָא must be tithed.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned: The unripe figs of בית הִינֵי and the dates of טוֹבִינָא are obligated in מעשר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the משנה that רבי יהודה is pointing to. It shows where the figs of בית הִינֵי are actually discussed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These figs and dates never fully ripen, so one might think they are not real produce and do not need tithing. The משנה rules that they are still eaten and must be tithed. That is the 'mention' רבי יהודה means.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה
A type of date that does not fully ripen
A place (Tovyana) known for these dates

phrases.english: As we learned:
The unripe figs of Beit Hini
and the dates of Tovyana —
are obligated in tithes.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּתְנַן: פַּגֵּי בֵּית הִינֵי וַאֲהִינֵי דְטוֹבִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for רבי יהודה's claim
steps.raayaObject: רבי יהודה's claim that בית הִינֵי figs appear only in the laws of מעשר
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה ruling that the figs of בית הִינֵי and the dates of טוֹבִינָא must be tithed

steps.title: The deadline for eating dates
steps.stepSummary: Dates may be eaten until the last ones in צוער are gone. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל adds that only dates among the palm branches count, not dates among the thorns.
steps.simpleTranslation: One may eat dates until the last ones in צוער are finished. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: one may eat based on those between the palm branches, but not based on those between the thorns.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues its list of deadlines with dates. The marker is צוער, where dates last the longest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion uses the last dates in צוער as the end point. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל narrows what counts as 'still there'. Proper dates growing among the branches extend the time, but a few stray dates stuck among the thorns do not.

keyTerms.meaning: Tzoar, a place where dates ripen late

phrases.english: One may eat dates
until the last one in Tzoar is finished.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
One may eat based on those between the palm branches,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין אוֹכְלִין עַל שֶׁל בֵּין הַשִּׁיצִין.
phrases.english: but one may not eat based on those between the thorns.

steps.triggerLanguage: אוֹכְלִין בִּתְמָרִים עַד שֶׁיִּכְלֶה הָאַחֲרוֹן שֶׁבְּצוֹעַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of fruit deadlines with dates
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dates may be eaten until the last ones in צוער are gone. Per רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, only dates among the branches extend the time.

steps.title: Another source gives fixed holiday deadlines
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא sets deadlines by holidays: grapes until פסח, olives until עצרת, dried figs until חנוכה, dates until פורים. רבי יוחנן switches the last two.
steps.simpleTranslation: They contrasted it: One may eat grapes until פסח, olives until שבועות, dried figs until חנוכה, and dates until פורים. רב ביבי said: רבי יוחנן switches the last two.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a contradiction. A different ברייתא gives calendar dates instead of places.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our ברייתא ties the deadline to when the fruit runs out in a certain place, and for dates that place is צוער, where dates last very late. The other ברייתא gives a fixed holiday for each fruit. In רבי יוחנן's version, dried figs and dates are swapped, so dates last only until חנוכה. That seems to contradict the late צוער deadline for dates.

keyTerms.meaning: And they contrasted it (introduces a contradiction)

steps.confusionAlert: רב ביבי's line is not a new opinion about the law. He is only reporting רבי יוחנן's version of the same ברייתא, where dried figs and dates trade places.

phrases.english: And they contrasted it:
One may eat grapes until Passover,
olives until Shavuot,
dried figs until Chanukah,
dates until Purim.
And Rav Beivai said:
Rabbi Yochanan switches the last two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the place-based deadlines with a holiday-based source
steps.kashyaTarget: The place-based deadlines in the ברייתא, such as the last dates in צוער
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One source ties the deadline to fruit running out in a place. The other ties it to a fixed holiday. These seem to be two different measures.

steps.title: Both describe the same time period
steps.stepSummary: The two measures come out to the same time. The fruit in those places runs out right around those holidays.
steps.simpleTranslation: This and that are one measure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its first answer. There is no real contradiction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One ברייתא names the place and the other names the season. The last dates in צוער, for example, are gone at about the time of the holiday listed. Both describe the same deadline in different words.

phrases.english: This and that
are one measure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 14
steps.terutzResolutionType: Harmonization: both sources describe the same period
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The place-based deadline and the holiday deadline were thought to be two different times
steps.terutzMaskana: They are the same time, described once by place and once by calendar

steps.title: The real rule depends on whether fruit still exists
steps.stepSummary: Second answer: the ברייתא says outright that if later fruit exists somewhere, one may keep eating. So the places and holidays are only general guides.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you wish, say: it is taught explicitly, 'If there are later ones than these, one may eat based on them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a different answer. It points to a line in the ברייתא itself, first seen in Step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא already says that if fruit lasts longer somewhere else, eating may continue. So neither the named places nor the holidays are hard limits. The real test is whether the fruit is actually still found in the field.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces another answer)

steps.whatToRemember: The deadline for eating שביעית fruit really depends on whether that fruit is still found in the field. The named places and holidays are only general markers.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that ביעור is tied to real conditions in the field, not to a fixed calendar date.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
it is taught explicitly:
If there are later ones than these —
one may eat based on them.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא, הָא קָתָנֵי בְּהֶדְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, independent answer to Step 14
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual: the ברייתא itself says the markers are not absolute
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The listed places and holidays were thought to be fixed cutoffs
steps.terutzMaskana: Eating continues as long as fruit is actually found somewhere, so the markers are only guides
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The deadline follows the actual presence of fruit in the field

steps.title: Plants that show what kind of land it is
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל lists signs of land types: gallnut trees for mountains, palms for valleys, reeds for streams, and sycamores for the lowland.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: The sign of mountains is gallnut trees. The sign of valleys is palms. The sign of streams is reeds. The sign of the lowland is the sycamore.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a related ברייתא from רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. It moves from palm trees to a general list of which plants grow in which kind of land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each type of land has a typical plant that grows well there, so the plant tells you what kind of land an area is. The ברייתא does not say why this matters. The גמרא works out the practical uses in the steps that follow: בכורים, נחל איתן, and buying and selling.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: It was taught: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
The sign of mountains is gallnut trees.
The sign of valleys is palm trees.
The sign of streams is reeds.
The sign of the lowland is the sycamore.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: סִימָן לְהָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from palm-based deadlines to signs that identify regions
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each type of land is recognized by its typical plant: gallnut trees, palms, reeds, or sycamores

steps.title: A verse hinting that sycamores belong to the lowland
steps.stepSummary: There is no real proof, but a פסוק in מלכים hints that sycamores belong to the lowland.
steps.simpleTranslation: Although there is no proof for this, there is a hint, as it says: 'And the king made silver in ירושלים like stones, and he made cedars like the sycamores that are in the lowland, in abundance.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds a פסוק that hints at the sycamore sign. It says clearly that this is a hint, not a proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says sycamores are 'in the lowland', which matches the sign for שפלה. The phrase זכר לדבר tells us the verse is only a reminder. The rule does not stand on it.

keyTerms.meaning: There is no proof for the matter
A hint / reminder for the matter

steps.confusionAlert: זכר לדבר is weaker than a real proof. The ברייתא openly says the verse is only a hint.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין רְאָיָה לְדָבָר,
phrases.english: And although there is no proof for the matter,
there is a hint for the matter, as it is said:
"And the king made the silver
in Jerusalem like stones,
and the cedars he made like the sycamores
that are in the lowland, in abundance."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין רְאָיָה לְדָבָר, זֵכֶר לַדָּבָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a scriptural hint for the sycamore sign in Step 17
steps.raayaObject: The sign that sycamores mark the lowland
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלכים א י:כז, 'like the sycamores that are in the lowland', offered only as a hint

steps.title: Why the mountain and valley signs matter
steps.stepSummary: The signs for mountains (gallnut trees) and valleys (palms) matter for the laws of בכורים.
steps.simpleTranslation: A sign of mountains is gallnut trees. A sign of valleys is palm trees. The practical difference is for בכורים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what practical law depends on the signs for mountains and valleys. It answers: the laws of בכורים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Knowing the true type of a piece of land tells you whether a fruit grew in its proper place. That affects whether the fruit is good enough to bring as בכורים. The proof comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Gallnut trees (a type of oak), a sign of mountain land
Palm trees, a sign of valley land
The practical difference; what law depends on this
First fruits brought to the בית המקדש

phrases.english: A sign for mountains is gallnut trees,
a sign for valleys is palm trees —
the practical difference is for first fruits,
phrases.notes: The גמרא asks and answers its own unspoken question: why do we need these signs?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the practical purpose of the signs listed in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The mountain and valley signs matter for deciding which fruit may be brought as בכורים.

steps.title: Source: first fruits must come from their proper land
steps.stepSummary: A משנה rules that בכורים are not brought from palms in the mountains or from grain in the valleys.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: בכורים are brought only from the seven species. They are not brought from palms in the mountains, and not from produce grown in the valleys.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a משנה to show that the type of land matters for בכורים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בכורים must be the best fruit. Palms grow poorly in the mountains, and mountain crops grow poorly in the valleys. Fruit grown in the wrong kind of land is not choice fruit, so it cannot be brought. That is why we need the signs to identify the land.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה
The seven species Eretz Yisrael is praised for

phrases.english: As we learned in a mishna:
One does not bring first fruits
except from the seven species,
and not from palm trees that are in the mountains,
phrases.notes: Palms belong in valleys, so mountain dates are inferior.

phrases.english: and not from produce that is in the valleys.
phrases.notes: Produce suited to the mountains grows poorly in the valleys.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the claim in step 19.
steps.raayaObject: That the type of land matters for בכורים

steps.title: Why the stream sign matters
steps.stepSummary: Reeds show that a place is a stream. This matters for the נחל איתן of עגלה ערופה.
steps.simpleTranslation: A sign of streams is reeds. The practical difference is for the נחל איתן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why we need the sign for streams. It matters for the stream used in the עגלה ערופה ceremony.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a murdered body is found and the killer is unknown, the תורה requires breaking a calf's neck at a נחל איתן. Growing reeds help identify a place as a stream.

keyTerms.meaning: The rough stream where the עגלה ערופה is brought

phrases.english: A sign for streams is reeds —
the practical difference is for the rough stream.
phrases.notes: This refers to the עגלה ערופה in דברים, chapter כא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues listing practical uses for each sign.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Reeds identify a stream for the law of עגלה ערופה.

steps.title: Why the lowland sign matters
steps.stepSummary: Sycamores mark the lowland. This matters for buying and selling land.
steps.simpleTranslation: A sign of the lowland is the sycamore. The practical difference is for buying and selling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why we need the sign for lowland. It matters when someone buys or sells land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose a seller promises a field in the lowland. The land he delivers must actually be lowland. Sycamore trees show that it is.

phrases.english: A sign for the lowland is a sycamore —
the practical difference is for buying and selling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the last of the practical uses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The sycamore sign defines lowland in land sales.

steps.title: All the signs also matter for buying and selling
steps.stepSummary: Since buying and selling is a valid use, every one of the signs can serve that purpose too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that you have come to this, all of them are also for buying and selling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up the topic. Every sign, not just the sycamore, can matter for land sales.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא found separate uses for each sign. Then it noticed that one use, buying and selling, works for all of them. A sale of 'mountain land' or 'valley land' would also be judged by these signs.

keyTerms.meaning: Now that you have arrived at this

steps.whatToRemember: Each sign has its own use (בכורים, עגלה ערופה, sales), and all of them also apply to buying and selling land.

phrases.english: Now that you have arrived at this,
all of them are also for buying and selling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the use from step 22 and applies it to all the signs.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Buying and selling is a practical use shared by every land sign.

steps.title: Selling small animals to non-Jews follows local custom
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: where people sell small animals to non-Jews, one may sell them. Where they do not, one may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: In a place where they used to sell small animals to non-Jews, they sell. In a place where they did not, they do not sell.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lists more laws that depend on local custom, starting with selling small animals such as sheep and goats to non-Jews.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues the chapter's theme: follow the custom of your place. Some places were strict and did not sell small animals. The reasons will be discussed in the גמרא.

keyTerms.meaning: A place where they were accustomed
Small livestock, such as sheep and goats

phrases.english: MISHNA
A place where they were accustomed to sell
small livestock to gentiles — they sell;
a place where they were not accustomed to sell —
they do not sell.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָקוֹם שֶׁנָּהֲגוּ לִמְכּוֹר בְּהֵמָה דַּקָּה לַגּוֹיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New משנה; the topic shifts from land signs to local customs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling small animals to non-Jews depends on local custom.

steps.title: Large animals may not be sold anywhere
steps.stepSummary: In every place, one may not sell large animals, calves, or foals to non-Jews, whether healthy or injured.
steps.simpleTranslation: In every place, one does not sell them large animals, calves, or foals, whether whole or broken.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now gives a rule that does not depend on custom. Large animals may never be sold to non-Jews.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Large animals do work. חז"ל worried that the sale might be undone, and a Jew's animal would end up having worked on שבת. Even young or injured animals are included in the ban.
steps.confusionAlert: This rule is not about local custom. It applies everywhere, unlike the small animals in the previous step.

phrases.english: And in every place one does not sell them
large livestock,
calves or foals,
whether whole or broken.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבְכׇל מָקוֹם אֵין מוֹכְרִין לָהֶם בְּהֵמָה גַּסָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with step 24: this rule is universal, not dependent on custom.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Large animals may never be sold to non-Jews, even young or injured ones.

steps.title: Two opinions that allow exceptions
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה permits selling an injured animal. בן בתירא permits selling a horse.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה permits an injured one. בן בתירא permits a horse.
steps.whatsHappening: Two תנאים disagree with part of the ban. Each one allows a single exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה reasons that an injured animal cannot do work, so the worry about work on שבת does not apply. בן בתירא allows a horse, since it is used mainly for riding, and riding is not a מלאכה forbidden by the תורה.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda permits a broken one.
Ben Beteira permits a horse.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disputes the full ban of step 25 by carving out exceptions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה allows selling an injured animal. בן בתירא allows selling a horse.

steps.title: Eating roasted meat on פסח night follows local custom
steps.stepSummary: Where people eat roasted meat on פסח night, they may. Where the custom is not to, they may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: In a place where they used to eat roasted meat on the nights of פסח, they eat. In a place where they used not to eat it, they do not eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives another custom, this one connected to פסח night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Outside the בית המקדש, eating roasted meat on פסח night could look like eating the קרבן פסח in the wrong place. Some places avoided it for that reason, while others allowed it. Each place follows its own custom.
steps.whatToRemember: This משנה lists customs that vary by place: selling small animals and eating roasted meat on פסח night. Selling large animals is banned everywhere.

phrases.english: A place where they were accustomed to eat roasted meat
on the nights of Passover — they eat;
a place where they were accustomed not to eat —
they do not eat.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָקוֹם שֶׁנָּהֲגוּ לֶאֱכוֹל צָלִי בְּלֵילֵי פְסָחִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another custom-dependent law to the משנה's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating roasted meat on פסח night depends on local custom.

steps.title: רב forbids saying 'this meat is for פסח'
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quoting רב: a person may not say 'this meat is for פסח,' because it looks like he set aside his animal as a קרבן and is eating קדשים outside.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: A person may not say, 'This meat is for פסח.' It looks like he is setting his animal aside as a קרבן and eating holy meat outside the בית המקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its discussion of the משנה about roasted meat on פסח night. It brings a rule from רב about what a person may not say.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nowadays there is no קרבן פסח, but the words 'for פסח' sound like the words used to set aside a קרבן. So someone hearing them might think he is eating קדשים outside ירושלים, which is forbidden. The problem is how it looks, not what he is actually doing.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
Like someone who sets aside an animal as holy (a קרבן)
Holy sacrificial meat eaten outside the permitted area
It looks like (a concern about appearances)

steps.confusionAlert: רב is not saying the meat actually becomes holy. The only issue is that the words make it look that way.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
It is forbidden for a person to say
'This meat is for Pesach'
because he appears like one consecrating his animal
phrases.notes: As if he were designating a קרבן פסח

phrases.english: and eating consecrated meat outside.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: אָסוּר לוֹ לְאָדָם שֶׁיֹּאמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה about roasted meat on פסח night.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may not say 'this meat is for פסח,' since it looks like eating קדשים outside.

steps.title: רב פפא limits the rule to meat, not wheat
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא: the rule applies only to meat. Saying 'this wheat is for פסח' is fine, because it plainly means 'guard it for פסח.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: This is only about meat. But wheat is not a problem, because he obviously means 'watch this wheat for פסח.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא narrows רב's rule. It applies only to meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Meat can look like a קרבן, so the words 'for פסח' are confusing. Wheat cannot be a קרבן פסח, so everyone understands he means guarding it from חמץ for מצה.

keyTerms.meaning: To be guarded (kept from becoming חמץ)

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Specifically meat;
but wheat — no,
for he is saying it should be guarded for Pesach.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רב's rule to meat only.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ban covers meat only; saying 'this wheat is for פסח' is permitted.

steps.title: Challenge from תודוס of Rome
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: is it really forbidden to say about meat? It brings a ברייתא: תודוס of Rome had the people eat whole-roasted kids on פסח night, and the חכמים said that if he were not תודוס they would have put him in נידוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is meat really not allowed? The גמרא objects: רבי יוסי said: תודוס of Rome made it a custom for the Jews of Rome to eat young goats roasted whole on פסח nights. The חכמים sent him a message: If you were not תודוס, we would have put you in נידוי, because you are feeding the Jewish people קדשים outside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's rule that simply calling meat 'for פסח' is forbidden. It quotes a story about תודוס of Rome.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question 'ובשר לא?' asks whether it is really forbidden to say 'for פסח' about meat. In the story, the חכמים objected only because תודוס had people eat kids roasted whole (מקולסין), the way the קרבן פסח was prepared. On the next amud the גמרא reads this to mean that only מקולסין is a problem, so ordinary meat called 'for פסח' should be allowed. That contradicts רב's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection (usually from a ברייתא)
תודוס of Rome, an important leader there
Roasted whole, with the innards on the head, like the קרבן פסח

steps.confusionAlert: The challenge argues for leniency. The story suggests that only meat roasted whole like the קרבן פסח is a problem, so merely calling meat 'for פסח' should be allowed.

phrases.english: And with meat, is it not [permitted to say this]?
They raised an objection:
Rabbi Yosei said:
Todos of Rome instituted a custom
for the people of Rome to eat
kids roasted whole on Pesach nights.
They sent to him:
Were you not Todos,
we would have decreed a ban on you,
because you are feeding Israel
consecrated meat outside.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the רב/רב פפא rule that calling meat 'for פסח' is forbidden.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule (as limited by רב פפא) that saying 'this meat is for פסח' is forbidden.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The חכמים objected only to kids roasted whole (מקולסין), which look like the קרבן פסח. This implies that ordinary meat is not a problem, so simply calling meat 'for פסח' should not be forbidden, against רב.

steps.title: Questioning the word 'קדשים' in the story
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: how can the ברייתא say 'קדשים'? The meat was not actually holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: Could you really think it was 'קדשים'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses on the wording of the ברייתא. The meat in Rome was never set aside as a קרבן, so calling it 'קדשים' cannot be literal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody in Rome was eating real sacrifices. So the word 'קדשים' needs to be fixed. This sets up a correction of the text.

keyTerms.meaning: Could it enter your mind? (this cannot be meant literally)

phrases.english: 'Consecrated meat' — could that enter your mind?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions a word inside the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's phrase 'feeding Israel קדשים outside.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The meat was ordinary and never consecrated, so 'קדשים' cannot be literal.

steps.title: Setting up a corrected reading
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to fix the wording: 'Rather, say...' The corrected wording comes next.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is about to give a corrected version of the ברייתא's words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'אלא אימא' signals that the text should be read differently. The new wording, which comes in the next lines, will explain what the ברייתא really meant instead of 'קדשים.'

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say (read the text this way instead)

phrases.english: Rather, say:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the wording question about 'קדשים.'
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא literally says תודוס fed people real קדשים.
steps.terutzMaskana: The wording will be corrected in the next lines to describe something that only looks like קדשים.
